setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a} and are doing the closing count of {supply.plural}. Your count is 6 lower than the log shows.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are counting {supply.plural} at closing. You count 6 fewer than the log says there should be.
pressure: {coworker3} says everyone wants to go home and you should just wrap it up.
It is already past closing time.
detail: The {supply.plural} are stored on the top shelf.
The rest of the closing tasks are done.

tiers.1: A false record cannot be fixed later; honesty comes first.
tiers.2: The procedure's check confirms the problem before it is reported.
tiers.3: Your own part in the problem belongs in the report.
tiers.4: The report has to reach the person the procedure names.

fact: {coworker} suggests changing the count sheet to match the log so nobody gets questioned.
issues.short: the suggestion to change the count
issues.action: Record the real count, and decline to change the numbers.
issues.brief: record the real count and decline to change it
issues.reason: A count sheet that hides a shortage is a false record. Accurate numbers are what let the team find the cause.
issues.lesson: Record what you actually find, even when the honest number leads to questions.

shortcut.text: Change the count to match the log, since a few items are not worth the trouble.
shortcut.brief: change the count to match the log
shortcut.why: Changing the numbers creates a false record and hides a real problem from the people who need to know.
shortcut.mis: Small differences are not worth reporting honestly.

fact: The posted closing procedure says a second person must recount any shortage.
clear: {coworker2} already recounted, and the second count matched yours.
issues.done: the second count was already done
issues.action: Ask {coworker2} to do the second count that the procedure requires.
issues.reason: The procedure's second count confirms the shortage is real before it is reported.
issues.lesson: Follow the procedure's check steps before reporting a problem.

shortcut.text: Skip the recount, since you are sure your own count is right.
shortcut.why: The procedure requires a second count. Skipping it breaks the procedure and leaves room for error.
shortcut.mis: Your own count is accurate enough to skip the procedure.

fact: You remember handing out several {supply.plural} today without writing them in the log.
issues.short: the items you handed out without logging
issues.action: Include the items you handed out without logging when you report the count.
issues.brief: report the items you did not log
issues.reason: Your unlogged handouts may explain the shortage. Being open about your own slip helps solve it and keeps your word trustworthy.
issues.lesson: Be open about your own mistakes, especially when they may explain a problem.

shortcut.text: Leave out the unlogged items so the shortage does not look like your fault.
shortcut.why: Hiding your part leaves the team chasing the wrong cause and damages trust if it comes out later.
shortcut.mis: Admitting a mistake will only get you in trouble.

fact: {Lead|the} has gone home, and the posted procedure says the on-call manager handles shortages after hours.
issues.short: who should receive the report tonight
issues.action: Report the shortage to the manager on call, as the procedure says.
issues.brief: report it to the manager on call
issues.reason: The procedure names who receives shortage reports when the lead is out. Following it gets the report to someone who can act tonight.
issues.lesson: Send reports to the person the procedure names, even when it is not your usual supervisor.

shortcut.text: Leave a note for {lead|the} to read in the morning instead.
shortcut.brief: leave a note for the morning
shortcut.why: The procedure says the on-call manager handles shortages tonight. A morning note delays the report.
shortcut.mis: Your usual supervisor is always the right person to tell.

proceed.text: Report the real count, including the shortage, to {lead|the}.
proceed.why: The count is confirmed and nothing else needs handling first, so the honest next step is to report it.
proceed.lesson: Report accurate results to the person responsible, even when they show a problem.

generic.text: Leave the count sheet blank and let the morning shift sort it out.
generic.why: An empty count sheet hides the problem and passes your job to someone else.
generic.mis: If a result is awkward, it is better not to record it.

generic.text: Keep recounting until your number matches the log.
generic.why: Counting until you get the answer you want is not an honest count.
generic.mis: The log is always right, so the count must be wrong.

overcaution.text: Hold the count sheet until {lead|the} can recount everything personally tomorrow.
overcaution.why: The count has already been checked. Holding it back delays a report the team expects tonight.
overcaution.mis: Only a supervisor's count can be trusted.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, counting {supply.plural} at closing, and the count is lower than the log.

recount: The posted procedure requires a second person to recount shortages.
owncause: You handed out some items today without logging them.
oncall: {Lead|the} has left, and shortages go to whoever is on call.

steps.text: Count every item on the shelf
Write the real number on the sheet
Add a note about the unlogged handouts
Check who is on call tonight

rel: The recount checks a first count, so the first count comes first.
The confirmed number is what goes on the sheet.
You write down the number after counting.
The note explains the number on the sheet.
The report should include your note.
You need to know who to report to before reporting.
The report is based on the written count.
process.lesson: Count, confirm, record honestly, explain your part, then report to the right person.

title: Closing count report: {supply.plural}
intro: You are checking this closing count report before it is filed.
doc.lesson: An honest report records what was found, follows the check steps and sticks to facts.

lines.fine: The log figure is recorded for comparison.

bad.why: The report shows 44 counted against 50 in the log. Saying there is no difference makes the record false.

lines.fine: The required second count is recorded.

bad.text: Second count: skipped, since the first count was probably right.
bad.why: The procedure requires a second count for shortages. Skipping it breaks the procedure.

lines.text: Note: I handed out 4 without logging them earlier today.

bad.text: Note: the shortage was most likely caused by the new hire.
bad.why: Nothing in the report supports blaming a person. A report should state facts, not guesses about who is responsible.

lines.text: Reported to the manager on call at 9:15 p.m.
lines.fine: Records who received the report and when.

bad.text: Changed the count to 50 so it matches the log.
bad.why: Changing the count falsifies the record and hides the shortage.

review.notes: Recount and on-call reporting are stated as posted procedures. No legal claims.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, partway through a normal shift.
pressure: Nobody else is around to see what you do.
detail: You have about an hour left in your shift.

fact: A friend asks you to use {system|the} to look up a neighbor's contact details.
issues.short: the request to look up a neighbor
issues.action: Decline, and explain that work records are only used for work.
issues.reason: Looking up someone's details for personal reasons misuses access you were given for your job.
issues.lesson: Use access to records only for the work it was given for.

shortcut.text: Look it up quickly, since the friend will not share it with anyone.
shortcut.why: The access is for work only. Using it for a friend is a misuse, whatever happens next.
shortcut.mis: Access is fine to use as long as nothing bad happens.

fact: A friend asks you for the staff discount, which the posted policy limits to employees.
issues.short: the request for the staff discount
issues.action: Politely explain that the staff discount is only for employees.
issues.reason: The policy is clear, and applying it the same way for everyone is fair. A polite explanation keeps the friendship and the rule intact.
issues.lesson: Apply workplace policies the same way for friends as for everyone else.

shortcut.text: Give the discount quietly, since it is only a few dollars.
shortcut.why: The amount does not change the policy. Bending rules for friends is unfair to others.

fact: {coworker} suggests you both take home some {supply.plural}, since there are plenty.
issues.short: the suggestion to take supplies home
issues.action: Leave the supplies, and point out that they belong to the workplace.
issues.reason: Workplace supplies are not personal property, even when there are extras.
issues.lesson: Treat workplace property as belonging to the workplace, even when there is plenty.

shortcut.text: Take a few, since nobody will miss them.
shortcut.why: Whether anyone notices does not change who owns the supplies.
shortcut.mis: If nobody notices, it is not really taking.

fact: A {client} offers you $20 in cash as thanks, and the handbook says staff may not accept cash gifts.
issues.action: Thank the {client} warmly and politely decline the cash.
issues.reason: The handbook does not allow cash gifts. A warm thank-you honors the gesture while following the rule.
issues.lesson: Follow gift rules politely; you can accept thanks without accepting the gift.

shortcut.text: Accept the cash quietly so the {client} is not offended.
shortcut.why: The handbook rule applies even when declining feels awkward. A sincere thank-you avoids offense.
shortcut.mis: Refusing a gift is always rude.

fact: Your time sheet shows 30 minutes you did not work, because you forgot to clock out yesterday.
issues.short: the extra 30 minutes on your time sheet
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} to correct your time sheet to the time you actually left.
issues.reason: Being paid for time you did not work is not fair to the employer. Fixing it yourself shows honesty.
issues.lesson: Correct records in your favor as readily as records against you.

shortcut.text: Leave the time sheet alone, since the clock made the mistake.
shortcut.why: You know the time is wrong. Keeping pay for time not worked is not honest, whoever made the error.
shortcut.mis: A mistake in your favor is not your responsibility.

proceed.text: Go along with it this once to keep things friendly.
proceed.why: Going along with the request would only be fine if no rule or fairness issue were involved.
proceed.lesson: Integrity means doing the right thing even when going along would be easier.

generic.text: Ask {coworker3} what they usually do and copy that.
generic.why: A coworker's habit is not the rule. The stated policy and honesty decide.
generic.mis: Whatever coworkers do must be acceptable.

generic.text: Say you will think about it and avoid the person for the rest of the day.
generic.why: Avoiding the question leaves it unresolved and is awkward for everyone. A clear, polite answer is better.
generic.mis: Avoiding a hard conversation makes it go away.

title: Tips from {coworker3} for your first week
intro: {coworker3} sent you these first-week tips. One of them is bad advice.
doc.lesson: Good workplace habits keep records accurate, property respected and rules applied fairly.

lines.text: Welcome to the team! Here are a few tips for your first week.
Clock in and out at the times you actually start and stop.
lines.fine: Accurate time records are basic honesty.

bad.text: If you forget to clock out, just leave it; it all evens out.
bad.why: Time records must be accurate. Leaving a wrong time means being paid for time not worked.

lines.text: Supplies stay here, even when there are extras.

bad.text: Extra {supply.plural} are fair game to take home.
bad.why: Workplace supplies are not personal property, even extras.

lines.text: Only look up records you need for your own work.
lines.fine: Access is for work purposes only.

bad.text: You can look up anyone in {system|the} if you are curious, as long as you keep it to yourself.
bad.why: Looking at records without a work reason is a misuse of access, even if nothing is shared.

lines.text: The handbook in the break room says staff may not accept cash gifts.
lines.fine: Accurately points to the written rule.

lines.text: If a {client} offers cash as thanks, thank them and politely decline.

bad.text: If a {client} hands you cash as thanks, keep it quietly.
bad.why: This contradicts the handbook rule mentioned in the same message. Cash gifts must be declined.

lines.text: Ask {lead|the} whenever a rule is unclear.

review.notes: Each rule (discount, gifts) is stated as workplace policy in the scenario. Issues are beginner-only because these requests would not naturally arrive together.

kits.familyName: Honesty and credit on a shared report
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You and {coworker} prepared {document|a} that {lead|the} will review tomorrow.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are finishing {document|a} with {coworker} for {lead|the} to review tomorrow.
pressure: {coworker3} says nobody checks these details anyway.
The review is first thing tomorrow morning.
detail: The document is saved in the shared folder.
You worked on it for about a week.

tiers.1: Accurate information comes before everything else.
tiers.2: Fair credit has to be set right before the review.
tiers.3: Your own errors should be fixed and admitted.
tiers.5: Being honest about what is unchecked comes once the content is right.

fact: {coworker2} suggests changing one number so the results look better.
issues.short: the suggestion to change a number
issues.action: Keep the real number and explain that the results must stay accurate.
issues.reason: Changed results mislead everyone who relies on the report.
issues.lesson: Report results as they are, even when they disappoint.

shortcut.text: Change the number slightly, since it is only one figure.
shortcut.why: Changing even one number makes the report false.
shortcut.mis: Small changes to data are harmless.

fact: {Lead|the} has thanked only you, though {coworker} did half the work.
issues.action: Tell {lead|the} that {coworker} did half the work.
issues.reason: Letting someone else's work be credited to you is unfair and dishonest.
issues.lesson: Give credit where it is due, even when nobody would notice.

shortcut.text: Accept the thanks, since {coworker} did not mention it.
shortcut.why: Staying silent takes credit for work you did not do.
shortcut.mis: Credit belongs to whoever is thanked.

clear: {Lead|the} already knows {coworker} did half the work.
issues.done: the lead already knows who did the work

fact: You find a mistake you made in your section.
issues.action: Fix the mistake and tell {coworker} what you changed.
issues.reason: Fixing it openly keeps the report accurate and keeps your partner informed.

shortcut.text: Fix it quietly so nobody knows there was a mistake.
shortcut.why: Fixing it is good, but hiding the change leaves your partner unaware of what changed.

fact: Part of your section copies a supplier's wording without saying where it came from.
issues.action: Credit the supplier's wording, or rewrite it in your own words.
issues.reason: Presenting someone else's words as your own is dishonest, even in a work document.

shortcut.text: Leave it, since suppliers want their wording used.
shortcut.why: Even if allowed, the words should be credited, not presented as yours.
shortcut.mis: Borrowed wording does not need credit at work.

clear: You already added a note crediting the supplier's wording.

fact: You will not finish checking the last section before the review.
issues.action: Tell {lead|the} which section has not been checked yet.
issues.reason: Being upfront about what is unchecked lets the lead judge how much to rely on it.
issues.lesson: Be honest about the limits of your work.

shortcut.text: Say the whole report is checked, since it probably is fine.
shortcut.why: Claiming checks you did not do is dishonest and risky.
shortcut.mis: Probably right is close enough to checked.

proceed.why: The report is accurate, credited and checked, so it is ready to send.
proceed.lesson: Send work forward once it is honest, accurate and fairly credited.

generic.text: Ask {coworker3} to send it under their name instead.
generic.why: Changing who sends it does not fix any problem and misrepresents who did the work.
generic.mis: Whoever sends a document gets the credit.

generic.text: Delay the review by saying the file was lost.
generic.why: Making up an excuse is dishonest.
generic.mis: A small lie is fine if it buys time.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to recheck every number before you send it.
overcaution.why: The report is already checked and accurate; a full recheck is unnecessary.
overcaution.mis: Nothing is honest until a supervisor checks it.

setup: You and {coworker} are finishing {document|a} at {workplace|the} for a review tomorrow.

error: You spotted a mistake in your own section.
copied: Some wording in your section came from a supplier.
unchecked: You will not have time to check the last section.

rel: Tell your partner after you make the change.
Your partner should know about the added credit.
Your partner should see the final version first.
The note goes in with the report.
process.lesson: Fix, credit, share changes, disclose limits, then send.

review.notes: Honesty and credit; no rules beyond general ethics are assumed.
